text: Okay. Hi, friends. I'm going to wait till everybody gets seated, but thank you all for being here. When we split up, I will have some of my friends at this table move over there just so that we have a balanced conversation, but you can stay put for now.

While we wait, I just wanted to share something with everybody. My 18-year-old son has autism, and we've had kind of a long journey in education, and he was accepted to his first choice for college today. And I am thrilled, and I just want you all to know how much you being here and advocating for your kids matters. It is because of 18 years of advocacy that we are where we

are, and it's important that you show up and let your voices be heard. It matters to all of our kids. So, thank you. And he's messaging me right now because he's supposed to be running his brother somewhere. Where is he going? Oh, he's going to Embry-Riddle. So, he's really into aviation, and he wants to go into aviation maintenance. So, yeah, I'm very excited for him.

Okay. Hopefully... I might have to go handle that. Okay. Good evening. We're going to officially get started. Thank you for joining us tonight. If you haven't done so already, please take a moment to sign in using the QR code at your table or in your agenda here. I call this meeting to order. Welcome to the November 16th, 2026 LEAF meeting. This meeting is officially in session. The first item on the agenda is public comment.

LEAF meetings are open to the public, and Loudoun County residents are welcome to attend. We kindly ask that all attendees refrain from interrupting the meeting's agenda to maintain a respectful and productive environment. Per the LEAF bylaws, public comments should address items on the agenda. If you wish to speak on an agenda item, now is the time to do so. There are no public comments, so we're going to move on. We need to approve the minutes from October 19th.

Hopefully, you had an opportunity to visit the LEAF website to review the minutes from last meeting prior to tonight's meeting. A printed copy is also included in the meeting materials at your table. I will now entertain a motion to approve the minutes from the October 19th, 2026 meeting as submitted. Is there a motion? Thank you. Amelia. Name. What's your first and last name? Amelia Kelsey.
Okay. Is there a second? Great. All in favor? Great. All opposed? The meetings are approved as submitted. At this time, I'm going to move things around. Hold on just a second.

We're going to introduce LCPS Superintendent, Dr. Aaron Spence. Thank you for taking the time to join us this evening. There will be time for questions at the end, and please remember that you're representing your communities at this meeting and keep comments and questions focused on those issues and concerns. Dr. Spence. Well, thank you. Good evening. It's so nice to be here with you all.

I will begin by apologizing for not having been able to be here last time, but I'm glad that we were able to make tonight work. I want to echo what Brooke said about the importance of your voice, and we'll talk a little bit about that in terms of advocacy tonight when you hear from our team about our legislative agenda. But these relationships really matter to us, and I'm going to talk about some information that we're finding out about these relationships. So,

at the back of the room, and you can certainly grab one on your way out if you have interest, we have put out our annual report, which we call our Innovation and Achievement Report. And so this is the one from the last school year, which is '25, '26. And I want to talk just for a little bit about what's in this report. I hope you'll take some time to take a copy and look through it. It's also available on our website in an interactive format. But I think it tells an important story

about the work that's happening across our school division. By the way, I'm a little distracted, because there's a balloon that's sitting up there on a heat source. Which is not great. So, if it pops, know everything is okay. It's just that I'm concerned it's going to, because it's literally sitting against a light. So anyway, if you can't tell, I have undiagnosed ADHD, and it's okay. Yeah, I know.

And I'm so glad to hear about your son. My son also is into aviation, so we're waiting to hear back from his schools. So- Anyway, I want to talk about this report. So the first thing is, I think it's always important for us as a school division to talk about how the investment that our community makes in us is paying off and returning what you all expect for us to be doing. So I'm also very competitive, and

so I love to brag about our school district and about some of the great things that we're doing just in terms of student achievement. So I'll just start there. And I'll just tell you, if you dig into what's in this report, what you're going to find out is that we continue to see growth and improvement in our test scores across the division, across all of our reporting categories. And just for context, we are the highest achieving large division in the Commonwealth of Virginia,

and we are outperforming all of our colleagues here in Northern Virginia with, I think, the exception of Falls Church, which is about 300 kids. Count them if you'd like. We don't. No, I'm just kidding. They're very nice people. And so we're very pleased by those results. And we should be, I think we have a lot to, as we look around instructionally at what we're doing in Loudoun County schools, a lot to be really proud of. Obviously, always more work to do.

My motto, "Be better tomorrow than you are today," and that always applies. And, I think we at least can point on the academic side and say, our kids do really well. And that's because of the hard work that we do every single day in our classrooms. That's because of the partnership that we have with our parents and families. Whenever I talk to people and they say, "What's the most important thing you can do to improve a school system?" I always start with, engage your families. Make sure that your families are working alongside their teacher,

that they're having conversations because you all know your kids way better than we know your kids, and it's helping us come to understand them and their learning needs that really makes us better at what we do. And so I think that that is critically important. And we talk a lot about that in here, too. We talk a lot about family engagement and our efforts there, and I'm going to get into that in a second. But before I do, I want to get into another piece that's in this report, which is about belonging.

So we talk a lot about belonging in LCPS. It's one of the core messages that I believe in when I work in a school system is as we shift culture, we shift towards a culture of belonging and care. And people sometimes look sideways at me like, "Well, why don't you just focus on the basics?" And what I usually tell them is you can't learn if you don't feel safe. You can't learn if you don't feel like you belong. And there's a lot of psychological evidence behind that.

Basically, I think all of us understand that learning is a social interaction. We learn from and with each other, and if you don't feel like you're supposed to be in that space and you don't feel included, it's very difficult to engage as a learner. And so we focus a lot on belonging and just wanting our students to know, whoever you are, whatever you bring with you, however you show up as your authentic self, you are welcome in our schools and in our classrooms. We want you here. You're supposed to be here. And so we talk a lot about how we build the conditions for that because that

doesn't just always come naturally, right? We're all human beings. This is a human business, and sometimes human beings exclude people for various reasons, and we have to get away from that and towards inclusion. What I was really proud of and what we've reported on in here is we ask questions about belonging. We specifically ask our students questions about belonging in that annual survey that you all know and love so much when you get it every year. And we

have a set of what we call our belonging questions that our data people have developed. And, what I would say is that 9 out of 10 of students in LCPS report that they feel a sense of belonging here, and I think that's really remarkable. And when you look at the specific numbers across our different levels, it's really great. So 92% of our elementary students report that. Eighty-four percent of our high school students, which is lower than you might want, but it's way higher than you'll see in many places.

Eighty-four percent of our high school students saying they feel like they belong. And our middle school students, over 90% of our middle school students say where they belong. Now, do any of you have middle school students? So you know what I'm talking about when I say like how remarkable it is that that number of middle school students are willing to say, "I feel like I belong here." And what I love about working in LCPS, and I've always loved about being here, is when I go into our schools, I can feel that. You can feel that when you're with our students.

And you can feel that just in the vibe and the culture of the building and how our teachers are interacting with our students. Now, again, does it mean every day, every child is feeling that? It doesn't. Obviously, the numbers indicate there are some who aren't. And so we know that continues to be part of our work and what we have to do to continue to be better. But I would say overall know that even when we might be missing the mark, it is our goal to make sure that when kids walk in, they know that they're loved

and that they're cared for and that they're supposed to be there and that the adults want them there because that's the core foundation to learning. Feeling safe physically, having your needs met, and then that psychological safety that comes with love and belonging that we all need to be great humans. So I love that that's in there. There's a whole other list of achievements and things that I would encourage you to celebrate and go forth and be our

good news carriers for us. I always think, sometimes in school systems, we're our own worst enemy. We get onto one issue that we just don't like, and we talk about that a lot, and all of a sudden, it's like the worst place you could ever send a kid. And our teachers do this as well, and I always remind people, step back from that and take a look at the big picture, and let's talk about the good things so that people realize most of what we do is good, and then we just have some challenges that we have to keep working on together.

I do want to reflect on one other thing that was really important to me. When I came into LCPS little over three years ago, I did a listening tour. Some of you maybe got a chance to come to that. And I just went to every high school, and I met with every faculty in that cluster and any parents who wanted to come into that meeting. And I listened a lot and heard a lot. And one of the things that

I found pretty heartbreaking back then was the folks who would say things like... I remember very specifically one faculty member who said, "You know, I've been here for 20 years, and we used to be so proud to work in LCPS, and I don't feel that way anymore." And we would have families who say, "We just want to trust LCPS again. We just want to feel like you care about our kids." And we measure also, if some of you in business maybe do this as well, we

measure net promoter scores. So basically, would you tell other people that you like working here? Would you tell other people they should send their kids here and feel good about that? And what I'm really pleased about also is our staff net promoter score in the last three years has gone up 40 points, and our family net promoter score has gone up 10 points. And so it tells me that we're doing a good job of building those bridges. And of course, it tells me we still have more work to do there, too. But

that's what we want. We want people to say, "Yeah. You know what? You're moving up to Northern Virginia. You need to send your kids to Loudoun County because they're going to have the best possible experience they can have." And we believe that, and we're working hard to make that a part of who we are and what we do. And I recognize and understand that a lot of that work happens outside of our classrooms. A lot of that work happens through our family engagement that we do through meetings like this, where we talk about what's going on and we sort out what's happening and try

to make ourselves better. We have a group of people who do that work every day, engaging with our families. I don't know if you know. Do you guys know who our family liaisons are? Are you familiar with them? Yeah, they're pretty amazing folks. One of the things that I wanted just to share in terms of some of the numbers also from this past school year about that group of people are family liaisons who work, as you know, with our parents, with community organizations,

to really connect students and families with the supports that they need because, again, you got to have support if your child's going to come to school and learn. They logged 71,000 hours last year supporting students and families. They had 50,000 instances of student intervention and support, and they had 31,000 instances of family support. So our family liaisons are really on the ground doing that incredible work. We're also building out partnerships. We just had an interfaith luncheon, our second interfaith luncheon, talking about

the ways that they can support our schools and our families. We now have 2,300 registered business partners across the division. That number has doubled over the last two years, and so because we've said, "Look, we're open for business, and we want to bring people together to support our kids and give our kids the opportunities that they deserve." And so these numbers represent those relationships, and they represent opportunities to take barriers away from our students and our families

so that as we're navigating challenges, we can work together to do that as a whole community. And I think that's worth celebrating, and I think this report is a reflection of that collective effort that we're engaged in. Something I want to share that we're also working on, because I just think it's really cool, and it's worth you all knowing about, and it's worth your schools that you're representing knowing about, is in the next school year, we're going to be opening something called the FACE Hub. So you know FACE stands for Family and Community Engagement.

And so it is actually a way that we are going to try to centralize and support the work of our family liaisons. It actually came out of an interfaith luncheon that we had last year where I was sitting at a table with two women from this wonderful church, and they said, "We can't even walk through the hall in our church because it's so full of backpacks that we have that people have donated that they want us to give to kids." And I thought, "Well, we can help with that. We should be able to find a central place where we can get all of those resources

coming together, where we can then build a distribution network to get those resources out to the families and students who need them." And we have Natalie Allen, who heads up our DCE and her team, but especially Renee Dawson, who you'll hear from, I think, in a little while, who heads up our FACE team. And they just ran with it. And they're like, "Yeah, we can do that." And we now have had our school board approve the building out of this hub

that is going to be a staffed hub with a warehouse distribution network. And so we're going to be able to really continue to grow our ability to meet the needs of our families. And that need is growing. It's growing here in Loudoun rapidly, quite frankly, more so than I think many people suspect. And as we look at our field program through the Loudoun Education Foundation, they're now delivering 1,500 to 2,000 meals a week to families.

And so we want to be a part of helping to support them and all of the needs that folks have. So we're grateful for that, and I would say, hey, families, stay involved with us on that as well because your neighbors are in need, and we're here to also help be a part of that. And I've also had some people say, "Why do you guys do that? You don't have to do that. Other people do that. The county does that. The food bank does that." We all have to do that because we do know, we all know if our kids

aren't coming to school ready to learn, they're going to continue to fall further behind. And so sometimes, we just need to step in and be a part of solving that problem and that challenge. I also, before I stop talking and take your questions, just want to give a brief update. It's always good to Make sure our families are engaged in the budget process and in the budget conversations that are happening. So we're in the midst of the budget cycle.

We've started having those priority conversations with our school board. And very quickly here, we're going to get some numbers coming out of the state, and the governor will recommend a budget for the next year here in the next couple of weeks. And then in January, we're going to present, so right after the winter holidays, we're going to present our recommended budget to the school board. So it's going to happen real fast. And there's things that I want to mention about it as we talk about it, because you

may have questions about things that we've talked about, and I'm happy to address those. But some of the things we're wrestling with as we look ahead at the budget, so you probably have seen or heard something about enrollment decline in LCPS, and that's a pretty significant issue across the Commonwealth, definitely in Northern Virginia, but it's also a national issue. And it's happening for a lot of different reasons. The primary reasons in Loudoun that we can identify

start with birth rate. So birth rate is always a driver of, I mean, if they're not being born, they don't come into our schools. And we're seeing a lower birth rate and a later birth rate. So families are choosing to have children later. And so that's an interesting dynamic that impacts our elementary schools. Housing affordability continues to be a conversation. So what we basically see is two things going on at the same time.

With high interest rates, we're not seeing a lot of turnover in the housing market, and we're seeing the aging out of a lot of our neighborhoods. So what I mean when I say aging out is the students have all graduated from high school and the families are staying put. And so there's not an opportunity for another family to come in with kids who are school-aged and live in that home. And then the homes that are being built and are available, as you all know, the median home price in Loudoun County is now over $800,000.

And so I don't know if you all remember being young. It's a vague memory for me. But I do know this. When I had little people, that wasn't going to be in my price range. And I think that if we understand that, we understand what some of our challenges are that are facing us. So in actual numbers, if you look at our projected enrollment for this year and our projected enrollment for next year, it's over 2,000 students difference. It's not the same for actual, so our

actual numbers are a little bit different. But it's a big drop. It's a big decline in overall student enrollment. We think there's other things going on. The loss of federal jobs is impacting us. We think some of the immigration policies are impacting us, and I'm not saying that to be political. I'm saying that because we know specifically a large population that's not in our schools this year are our EL students, and so we're seeing a significant decline in that group of students. And that's for the first time in a while.

That number has been on the rise for the last decade or so and is now declining a little bit. So we just think there's a myriad of things that are all coming together at the same time. And what that means for us generally is a couple of things is one is we receive money from the state based on a per pupil allocation, and we also staff our buildings based on the number of students who are in those buildings. And so when we see enrollment declines, it means there's going to be

changes to staffing in a school. It means a little bit less revenue anticipated from the state. And then all of that to say the sky's not falling. Sounds like it when you talk about it that way, but the sky is not falling because we also have a robust economy here in Loudoun County and in Northern Virginia in general. And the local revenue picture is still good. And so we're going to be okay, but what it does mean is it's tightening the resources that are available to meet our needs.

And so we first and foremost want to take care of our people. We have a union, and we have a collective bargaining agreement where we have negotiated compensation, and so the first thing we'll do is we'll deal with that. And then we'll look at our staffing, and we really want to, and I've said this to our staff, we want to ensure the people who are working here today who want to be working here next year will be here, and that's our goal. So we want to make sure that we build out a staffing model in the budget that

allows that to happen. So any staffing reductions we're going to try to do through normal attrition, things like people retiring or moving out of the county that we see every year. And then we'll look at other things. So compensation and benefits first, maintaining the staffing. Not necessarily maintaining all of the staffing that we have, but keeping the people that we have now that want to be here next year. And then we'll get into meeting the commitments that we have in some of our

programming. So we've opened the Academy for Global Linguistic Studies. We're still growing our IB program. Our HAMS, our Health and Medical Sciences programs are coming into their last years with staffing needs. And so looking at all of that and taking care of those ongoing commitments, we're also making adjustments for inflation. I don't know if you've noticed that your fuel bills have gone up. Ours have gone up a little bit. So we have a projected shortfall of about $2 million in our fuel budget this year. So we're

okay. We can manage that in a $2 billion budget. We just have to move things around to do so. And so next year, we'll have to budget for that. And so once you get to all of that, I guess what I'm saying is at the end of that, the money available to do new things or to meet the needs that we still perceive that our schools and our students have, it just gets a little tighter. And so there's going to be trade-offs and a lot of good conversation with our school board. And

what I would say is then I want to ask you to is to be a part of that process, to engage with your board members, to engage with us, and identify your priorities, and just know that there's going to be trade-offs as we run into what those priorities are that different groups have for each other. So that's kind of it around the budget and what we're up to these days. And I'm just going to stop there, and I'll take

any questions that you might have for a few minutes. Yes, ma'am. I'd really love to be starting with saying thank you for the professional interaction and doing this in terms of each other. With regards to the budget, I know it looks like we are increasing 60% to 80%. I think that's a very obvious place where we could save millions of dollars, particularly on the schools as far as I see any tangible fact. So is that

top of your mind for the budget next year? Yeah. And our board has identified that as part of their priorities, and so we're certainly looking at... I'm not sure if I heard it, but pretty sure you're talking about technology. Yeah. So, yes. You haven't seen it yet because we haven't brought forward a budget yet. We've just been starting initial conversations. Yeah, but it looked like you were making the ones on No. So

I would just encourage you to watch it again because we didn't say we-- Here's what we are doing. That was just a conversation about here's some of the things that we're thinking about. When I present the budget in January is where we'll really talk about what we're recommending. So the first presentation in January is where I present the estimate of needs, and that's where we're telling the board, "These are our recommendations." But to be sure, the board has signaled to us that one of their priorities is looking at device distribution, and internally, what I can tell you is we are absolutely looking at that.

The costs are extreme right now, to your point, 60% to 80% increases in technology costs. And so we want to make sure that we are both looking at the purpose of technology, making sure that it's intentional, productive, responsible use, looking at the age appropriateness of technology, and then figuring out are there cost savings associated with those two conversations in tandem, for sure. Yes, ma'am. Talking about feeling transparency, and that comes with LPS and all of that.

With going to the common assessments that we're kind of moving to and families can't really see any of that. So where you used to have it where the kids would take an assessment and then go over it with the teacher, and then it would go home so parents could look over it with them, maybe have a discussion at the dinner table. Now it seems that the kids are taking a

lot of assessments, but then we're not, as families, able to really see what that is. Is there a plan sort of in place to help maybe bridge that gap? And I can see it as both a parent and I'm also a teacher here in Loudoun, and I can see it from that lens as well. Are we thinking about how to bridge that so that parents are more involved with that?

Yeah, it's a great question. I have to be honest with regards specifically to the common assessments that we're now giving. It hadn't come up in conversation about that, so I appreciate you asking the question. What I'm going to do is jot it down, and I'm going to make sure I go sit with Ashley since you're here with our teaching and learning team and ask that question of how are we showing parents the results of those common assessments. So thank you for asking it.

Let me just jot down real quick. So what else is on your mind? So- Also, I'll just throw this out there because it just keeps coming up and I just want to put a nail in this one. As a part of the budget conversation, speaking about our October presentation, one of the things that we always do also is bring up when you think about enrollment decline, staffing is going to be a thing that we're going to look at.

We always bring up schools and whether or not we need to look at consolidating schools. That seemed to have stirred quite a bit of conversation, so I don't know if we've got anybody here from the west. And I just want to remind folks what we did was we just asked the board, "Do you want us to look into this further?" And the board said no. So we're not looking into that at this time. I will signal moving forward that we're going to be going through a district-wide rezoning on our secondary schools starting in the spring.

So looking at all of the secondary school attendance zones, that's going to come concurrent with the planned opening of a new high school in the Dulles area. High school 14, Thornton Summit, actually has a name now. I keep forgetting. Thornton Summit High School is going to be opening up. And so we got to rezone that one anyway, so the board said let's just do them all, take a look. And then the board has established a policy now where we look at them every five years. So one of the things we're going to have to do as we

think about enrollment is just make sure we right-size our buildings, and if enrollment decline continues, make sure that we're being good stewards of the resources that we do have. Okay. And I'm not sure if this is the appropriate venue, but I found myself talking with my teammate here earlier, before the meeting got started about something that has been on my mind lately. And that is, I work over here at Liberty Park Elementary. Our numbers dropped, I believe it might be 20, 25

students. But what that did is it triggered the situation where we lost a school counselor. And I want to preface this by saying I understand how businesses work. I understand that to change these numbers is probably hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not millions. A million-dollar decision. But I have a kid who has just minor anxiety, and they were getting small group- Mm-hmm ... time with their counselors last year.
And that counselor is one of the counselors, or the counselor that got pulled. She is not getting that

As a former teacher, I can only imagine because that's a big difference in workload. Sure. And so I think if this is the venue for that, I'd just like to say, I have been in the county, I do know mental health is something that at least in the past, when I was a teacher, we were focusing on, and I am seeing this firsthand thing where I don't know if when we are coming up with the budget, we can shuffle the numbers and make sure that maybe that number of per counselor is a little softer, maybe that's an important piece

to not just me, but other people. Yeah, no, it's the right venue. Absolutely, and that's part of the advocacy that I'm talking about. And it's also, frankly, part of the trade-offs that we're talking about, right? Because to your point, if you change the staffing number-- So everything, just, if you don't know generally how it works, we have a ton of positions that are linked to a staffing standard. So not every position, but we do have a lot of

our positions, and the staffing standard will say something like, "X number of teachers for X number of students, X number of counselors for a building that has X number of students." And if you go above or below that threshold, then we give you a counselor, or we take away a counselor, and that's what you've experienced. Right. And then what we do on an annual basis working with our board is we'll come, and we'll say, "Okay, here are our recommended staffing standards for the next year." And sometimes that's very strategic, so I'll give you a good example.

I just mentioned the number of EL students, the decline in our EL students. If I were to come with a budget in January that fairly represented our staffing standard for EL learners and EL teachers, we would lose 54 EL teachers overnight. So I'm probably not going to do that. What I'm going to do is try to be a little bit more strategic about that staffing standard and see if I can't adjust that so that we can handle that through attrition.

And so then that means, then do I have money to make an adjustment to our counseling standards? So those are the things we have to think about. I'm all for our counselors. I think they're amazing. I love what they do. I also, not I also, and I don't mean it to sound like excuse-making, we want to look and see how are we doing compared to other folks. And one of the things I know is we have a pretty good counselor-to-student ratio compared to most districts in the Commonwealth. And so then the question is, okay,

yes, it could be better. Where are the trade-offs? So know we'll think about it, but that truly is the kind of advocacy, and that's what your board members need to know. Hey, if you're making decisions about trade-offs, we prefer counselors above all else. And that helps- I would go that far. Yeah. I do think it's, and I- No, no. Yeah. It's really hard to swallow like, oh, you lost 15 kids, but now you're down a whole counselor. For sure. We have some positions

that we hold onto called flexible staffing positions for this reason, where our school leadership folks, like the executive principals, will work with their principals and say, "Yeah, you're five under, but maybe you're going to catch those up after the school year starts. Maybe we'll hold you harmless and keep that person in place." And so we do that. But it really is a conversation usually between the principal and leadership about whether or not we can afford a flexible staffing position there, and then the

other part of that is it's usually for one year, and then they got to figure out if they're getting it next year. Yeah, of course. No, I appreciate that. And no, this is absolutely the right place for that kind of advocacy. So thank you all for your time. I've got to run. I do have another commitment. But I appreciate the opportunity to be here. I always appreciate the opportunity to be with LEAF. I'm sorry it's as infrequent as it is, but we can do better. And I'm happy to come back during budget season and talk more about that if you all have interest.

Or if there are other topics of interest, I'm happy to come back and work with you on those as well. But I know I'm leaving you in great hands tonight with our team. You've got our folks that are going to talk about our legislative agenda. All I'll say on their behalf is, sometimes it's hard to be a prophet in your own land, and so when I'm standing up saying, "We need to fund education. We need to do this. We need to do that," they're like, "Oh, we keep hearing from this guy every year." We don't hear from anyone else. We'd really love for them to hear from other people.

Not them our board, them the folks in Richmond who do these things for us. So anyway, thank you all so much for your time. Appreciate you. Thank you. Thank you. Can I have that come back? Yes, you may. Sorry. Thank you. Thanks. Okay. Thank you, Dr. Spence. At this time, I'm going to welcome our school board representative, Ross Benson, to provide a school board update. We're going to go fast. I promised Brooke I would keep it brief.
